references.text: Moses applied blood to the horns of the altar and poured the rest at its base, as described in the priestly consecration ritual in Exodus.
The altar was cleansed and sanctified through the sin offering to make atonement, just as prescribed for the consecration.
The blood was smeared on the horns of the altar and the remainder poured out at the foot of the burnt offering altar, which was standard practice for sin offerings.
The priest took some of the blood from the sin offering and applied it to the horns of the burnt offering altar with his finger, following the same ritual that Moses performed.
Applying blood to the horns of the altar with a finger was a central part of the sin offering ritual for making atonement.
On the Day of Atonement, blood was smeared on the horns of the altar to cleanse and sanctify it from Israel's impurities.
Ezekiel describes that blood should be applied to the horns of the altar and poured out at its base to cleanse and make atonement for the altar.
For seven days, atonement was to be made for the altar, and it was to be cleansed and consecrated, parallel to the consecration ritual.
The book of Hebrews refers to how the tabernacle and all its vessels were cleansed with blood, and that under the law almost everything is purified with blood.
